A U.S. Navy wave energy test site located offshore from a Marine base in Hawaii tests marine energy technologies and connects to a land-based grid using underwater cables (SOEST 2025). In addition to other domestic deployments and demonstration projects, U.S.-headquartered company ORPC has developed river energy generation systems, deploying the RivGen Power System in a remote community in Alaska (ORPC 2025a) and testing a Modular RivGen Power System, including one in Maine in partnership with Sandia National Laboratories (ORPC 2025b; DOE WPTO 2024). Environmental risks from marine energy equipment and operation may present challenges or delays due to regulatory processes and requirements (Copping 2024), From a technological and investment perspective, marine energy deployment is still emerging, particularly in the United States, presenting uncertainties. E.5 Ocean Thermal Energy Conversion Ocean Thermal Energy Conversion (OTEC) technology generates electricity by using the difference in temperature between warm surface and cold deep ocean layers, typically requiring a 20°C difference (IRENA 2014, EIA 2023). Warm seawater is pumped through an evaporator containing fluid, and the vaporized fluid (either seawater or another fluid) drives a turbine while cold seawater condenses the vapor back to liquid. OTEC technology can be used for continuous electricity generation as well as cooling and desalination. 77 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies (NLR) at www.nlr.gov/publications. The technology is at demonstration scale, but high capital and operational costs and operational inexperience remain challenges (IRENA 2014). In part, high costs are driven by material needs (e.g., pipes) and the corrosive impacts of saltwater. Regions for the most effective deployment of the technology are tropical, 20 degrees north and south, given the requirement for warm surface water (Xiao and Gulfam 2023). Optimal OTEC deployment also requires deep water access, which may be considerable distances from shore in some tropical regions. In the United States, a 105-kilowatt (kW) demonstration facility is operational offshore of Hawaii; it was installed in 2015 and delivers electricity to the local grid (EIA 2023). The EU is developing and testing OTEC systems, including a demonstration project in the Canary Islands launched in 2024 (PLOCAN 2024). Additional recent demonstration projects include a 20-kW floating system and 50-kW systems, both deployed in China in 2023 (Su et al. 2025b). With OTEC systems still at demonstration scale and facing cost and optimal region limitations, the timeline for commercial-scale deployment is uncertain. E.6 Deployable Wind Energy Deployable wind turbines offer improved mobility and faster deployment compared to traditional wind turbines, with targeted applications for defense and disaster response (Summerville et al. 2022; NLR 2025a). These deployable systems range from small systems that are less than 3 kW and transported by backpacks or small trailers, to 10- to 20-kW systems that are transported by trailers or containers, to larger systems that are up to 100 kW to support larger electrical loads (Summerville et al. 2022).
